title: Data Structures in C
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs expect candidates to implement and reason about arrays, lists, trees, and hash tables from scratch in C using structs, pointers, and malloc.

phases.goal: Establish that C has no built-in containers and that core structures are built from structs, pointers, and heap allocation.

must_hit.point: C has no standard containers like vector or List; you build them from structs, pointers, and malloc.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States you shape data yourself with structs/pointers/malloc rather than using a standard library container type.

must_hit.point: A dynamic array struct tracks a heap pointer plus current length and capacity, and typically doubles capacity when full.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions data/len/cap fields and resizing by doubling when len equals cap.

must_hit.point: A singly linked list is a chain of self-referential nodes each holding a value and a next pointer, ending at NULL.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes head-to-tail pointer chasing and that you cannot jump to an arbitrary index.

must_hit.point: In a BST, for any node N all left-subtree values are less than N and all right-subtree values are greater than N.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the left < N < right ordering invariant clearly.

must_hit.point: A hash table maps keys to bucket indices via a hash function; collisions are commonly resolved with separate chaining (bucket linked lists).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains hashing into a finite bucket array and appending colliding entries to a per-bucket list.

probes: Why can't you use something like std::vector in C, and what three pieces of state does a dynamic array need?
What is the BST ordering rule, and how does a hash table handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?

hints.1: Think about what C gives you natively versus what you allocate and link yourself.
hints.2: Cover dynamic arrays (len/cap), linked nodes (next/NULL), BST left/right order, and hash buckets with chaining.
hints.3: Say: no built-in containers—use malloc/structs; vec has data/len/cap and doubles; list nodes end at NULL; BST left < N < right; hash collisions go into per-bucket linked lists.

phases.goal: Show how resize, pointer updates, BST delete cases, ring buffers, rehashing, and generics actually operate in C.

must_hit.point: When a dynamic array is full, allocate a larger block (often cap * 2), copy elements over (memcpy/realloc), and free the old block; amortized append is O(1) though a resize is O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through doubling, copy, free/realloc, and amortized O(1) vs occasional O(n).

must_hit.point: Before freeing a list node you must stash current->next; freeing first makes the rest of the list unreachable (Lost Node Trap).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says save next in a temporary, then free, then advance—never free then read next.

must_hit.point: BST deletion has three cases: leaf (parent to NULL); one child (relink parent to child); two children (replace with in-order successor—smallest in right subtree—then delete that successor).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all three cases and defines successor as smallest in the right subtree.

must_hit.point: A circular/ring buffer uses a fixed array with head and tail indices that wrap with modulo (%), giving O(1) enqueue/dequeue without shifting or malloc.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions fixed size, head/tail, wrap via %, no element shifting.

must_hit.point: When hash-table load factor (entries/buckets) exceeds a threshold (often 0.75), allocate a larger array and re-hash all keys into it.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines load factor and describes grow-and-rehash at about 0.75.

must_hit.point: Generic C containers hold void* and take function pointers (e.g. compare/free) because the container cannot interpret opaque element types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions void* storage plus callbacks like compare and free_element.

probes: Walk through appending to a full dynamic array, then deleting a singly linked list node safely.
How do you delete a BST node with two children, and when must a hash table rehash?

hints.1: Focus on what you save or copy before you free or overwrite a pointer.
hints.2: Order: resize copy path; stash-next-before-free; BST leaf/one/two-child; ring wrap; load-factor rehash.
hints.3: Double via cap*2 then memcpy/realloc; temp=next before free; two-child uses in-order successor; ring uses head/tail %; rehash past load factor often 0.75; generics need void* plus function pointers.

phases.goal: Compare structure choices for access, insert/delete, balance, and memory ownership.

must_hit.point: Linked lists excel at mid-sequence insert/delete via pointer updates with no shifting, but lose O(1) random access because nodes are non-contiguous.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts no-shift middle edits against pointer-chasing access versus arrays.

must_hit.point: A doubly linked list adds prev for bidirectional walk and O(1) deletion given a node pointer, at the cost of more pointer updates per operation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States bidirectional traversal and O(1) delete-if-you-have-the-node versus extra pointer management.

must_hit.point: Stacks/queues are ADTs: array-backed stacks push/pop at the end; list-backed queues keep head and tail pointers for dequeue/enqueue.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates LIFO/FIFO abstraction from array-end vs head/tail list backing.

must_hit.point: Unbalanced BSTs give O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced but degrade to O(n) if sorted inserts create a linked-list shape; hash tables target O(1) average lookup when log n is not enough.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions degeneration to a list and hash tables for average O(1) vs BST log n.

must_hit.point: Node-based ownership must be explicit: owning containers free element data in list_free; borrowing containers only free nodes and leave data to the caller—ambiguity causes leaks or double-frees.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes own vs borrow and ties mistakes to leaks/double-frees.

probes: When would you pick a linked list over a dynamic array, and when is a doubly linked list worth the extra pointers?
What goes wrong with a plain BST on sorted input, and how does that push you toward a hash table or a balanced tree?

hints.1: Compare random access and shifting costs first, then balance and ownership.
hints.2: Array vs list access/insert; singly vs doubly; stack/queue backing; BST skew vs hash O(1) avg; own vs borrow frees.
hints.3: List: mid insert without shift, no O(1) index; doubly: O(1) delete with node pointer but more links; sorted BST inserts -> O(n); hash for O(1) avg; document whether free walks element data.

phases.goal: Apply classic pointer and tree techniques used in interviews on these structures.

must_hit.point: Detect a list cycle with Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one step, fast moves two; meeting means a cycle, fast hitting NULL means none.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names Floyd / tortoise-hare and states one-vs-two step rules and both outcomes.

must_hit.point: Find the middle of a list with the same slow/fast pointer technique.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says slow/fast until fast ends; slow is at the middle.

must_hit.point: Iteratively reverse a singly linked list with three pointers (prev, curr, next): save next, reverse curr->next to prev, advance prev and curr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the three-pointer loop and returns prev as the new head.

must_hit.point: Validate a binary tree as a BST by tracking allowed min and max during recursive descent; build a queue using two stacks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions min/max bounds for BST validation and the two-stack queue construction.

probes: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list, and how do you reverse one in place?
How would you check that a binary tree satisfies the BST property?

hints.1: Interview classics here are mostly two-pointer list tricks and BST bounds.
hints.2: Cycle and middle use slow/fast; reverse uses prev/curr/next; BST check uses min/max ranges.
hints.3: Floyd: slow +1, fast +2, meet => cycle; reverse stashes next then flips link; validate BST with recursive min/max; queue from two stacks is another common ask.

tradeoffs.topic: Dynamic array vs singly linked list
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays give contiguous storage and O(1) index access but mid insert/delete costs O(n) shifting; linked lists insert/delete in the middle by updating a few pointers with no shifting, but access is O(n) pointer chasing and cache-unfriendly scatter.
Doubly linked lists add a prev pointer for bidirectional traversal and O(1) deletion when you already hold the node, at the cost of maintaining more pointers on every update.

An array-backed stack is a dynamic array restricted to end push/pop; a list-backed queue keeps head and tail so dequeue and enqueue stay efficient without shifting. In embedded settings without malloc, a fixed circular buffer with head/tail modulo wrap is preferred.

BSTs support ordered lookup and sorted in-order iteration at O(log n) when balanced, but sorted inserts can degenerate to O(n); hash tables aim for O(1) average search/insert/delete via hashing and chaining, without inherent sorted iteration.

If the structure owns element data, teardown must free each payload before freeing nodes; if it only borrows references, only node structs are freed and the caller frees data—unclear ownership causes leaks or double-frees.

gotchas.trap: Updating or freeing a list pointer before saving its successor (Lost Node Trap).
gotchas.correction: Stash current->next in a temporary before free or reassignment; e.g. never free(current); current = current->next.

gotchas.trap: Walking a list with the head pointer itself and losing the original head.
gotchas.correction: Use a separate current pointer for traversal so head remains usable.

gotchas.trap: Inserting already-sorted keys into an unbalanced BST (Degeneration Trap).
gotchas.correction: Recognize the tree becomes a linked list and search drops from O(log n) to O(n); production code uses self-balancing trees (e.g. AVL or Red-Black) for O(log n) depth.

gotchas.trap: Assuming hash lookup is always cheap without considering load.
gotchas.correction: Track load factor (entries/buckets) and when it exceeds a threshold (often 0.75), grow the bucket array and re-hash all keys.

gotchas.trap: Leaving memory ownership of node payloads unspecified.
gotchas.correction: Document whether the container owns or borrows data, and free accordingly to avoid leaks and double-frees.
